Derivatives of Sine and Cosine

CurvesLimitsComplex Analysis
Game: A point runs round a circle. Watch how its across-and-up arrows match the arrows of the direction it is moving.
How to play: Press Start, or drag the point round the circle. Try Slow and Fast.

blue: cos t   red: sin t

sin′(t) = cos(t),   cos′(t) = −sin(t)

Speed
Look for the math

A point turning round the unit circle is at r = (cos t, sin t). Its velocity r′ = (cos′ t, sin′ t) is tangent to the circle, so it is perpendicular to the radius:

cos t · cos′ t + sin t · sin′ t = 0,

which is also what you get by differentiating cos² t + sin² t = 1.

Two equal triangles

The radius, the blue cosine arrow and the red sine arrow make a right triangle. The velocity, split into an upright and a sideways arrow, makes another right triangle with the same sides, turned by a quarter turn. So the upward part of the velocity is as long as the cosine, and the sideways part as long as the sine. The logic test checked this at every whole degree. Notice how the order of the two velocity arrows flips four times in one turn.

Reading off the derivatives

The sine grows while the cosine is positive (on the right half of the circle) and falls while it is negative, at exactly the rate cos t: sin′ t = cos t. The cosine falls in the upper half, where the sine is positive, and grows in the lower half: cos′ t = −sin t. The test compared the velocity arrow with the change of (cos t, sin t) over a tiny step at all 360 angles.

Euler's formula

The picture also fits Euler's formula eit = cos t + i sin t. Differentiating as if i were an ordinary number gives (eit)′ = i eit, and multiplying by i turns a complex number a quarter turn: i eit = −sin t + i cos t, the velocity in the picture.

Stop at 45°, then at 135°. Which arrow of the velocity changes sides?
